title: Comparing change goals and feasibility beliefs about changing social, emotional, and behavioral skills vs. personality traits among adolescents, parents, and teachers
abstract: This study compared adolescents', parents', and teachers' change goals and feasibility beliefs for Big Five traits versus social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills. Participants were 676 Italian high school students who reported about themselves, 461 parents who reported about their participating child, and 704 international teachers reporting about students in general. We found that all groups viewed SEB skills as more changeable than traits, with the strongest skill preference among teachers. Student differences were clearest for Social Engagement versus Extraversion. Teachers, but not parents, also reported greater interest in skill-based than trait-based interventions. These findings suggest that skill framing may increase perceived malleability and support for developmental interventions in educational contexts. © 2026 The Authors
authors: Feraco, Tommaso and Jach, Hayley K. and Bardach, Lisa and Kopatz, Myriel and Murayama, Kou and Sewell, Madison N. and Napolitano, Christopher M. and Soto, Christopher J.
notes: Review-only. BESSI-derived change goals/feasibility beliefs do not measure SEB skill capacity. Sample characteristics intentionally not extracted.

title: Cognitive Abilities, Personality, and Sustainable Attitudes and Behavior
abstract: Climate change demands urgent action, yet individual engagement in sustainable behaviors remains inconsistent. We conducted two studies (N1 = 280, N2 = 973) examining how political orientation, personality traits, reasoning ability, social-emotional-behavioral skills, and complex problem solving relate to sustainable attitudes and behaviors in U.S. adults. Using structural equation modeling, we found that openness to experience was the strongest predictor, alongside liberal political orientation and self-perceived social engagement and innovation skills. Unexpectedly, both cognitive personality traits showed negative associations with sustainability outcomes, challenging the notion that cognitive abilities universally facilitate adaptive behavior. For sustainable behavior, these associations were small to moderate (-.25 <= r <= -.15) and most pronounced for food-related and engagement-related behaviors. Specification curve analyses confirmed that less established constructs (social, emotional, and behavioral skill self-concepts and complex problem solving) contributed meaningful variance beyond established personality predictors and that these associations were robust across analytical specifications. Overall, psychological characteristics together explained up to 44\\% of variance in sustainable attitudes and 29\\% of variance in sustainable behavior. These findings advance our understanding of the psychological underpinnings of environmental engagement and highlight the need for future research to clarify the mechanisms underlying the negative cognitive ability-sustainability association.
authors: Lubczyk, Till and Bleidorn, Wiebke and Hopwood, Christopher J. and Kretzschmar, Andre
notes: Only Study 2 proceeds to quantitative coding. Study 1 receives no quantitative sample or matrix ID.

title: From fragmentation to framework: defining core human competencies for higher education and the workplace
abstract: Purpose – This article addresses the lack of a coherent, shared language for human-centred competencies in higher education, introducing core human competencies (CHCs) and the 4S framework as an integrative alternative to fragmented terminology such as soft skills, transferable skills and 21st-century skills. Design/methodology/approach – A dual-strategy methodology was employed: a synthesis of leading international competency frameworks (CASEL, BESSI, CCR, OECD Learning Compass, 2030) combined with a structured bibliometric analysis of 880 Scopus-indexed publications (2009–2025), using VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence mapping across seven identified clusters. Findings – Fifteen core competencies were identified from frameworks and research clusters. These are organised into the 4S framework: Self-awareness, Self-leadership, Situational management and Social capacities, positioning CHCs as a holistic framework. Research limitations/implications – The framework is conceptual and requires psychometric validation, longitudinal testing and cross-cultural assessment. Future research should examine predictive validity, factor structure and applicability across disciplines and cultural contexts. Practical implications – The 4S framework offers higher education institutions a shared conceptual language for curriculum design, learning outcomes, pedagogy, staff development and institutional strategy. Originality/value – This article provides the first empirically informed synthesis producing a unified taxonomy of CHCs applicable across higher education contexts, reducing terminological redundancy and offering a practically useable developmental architecture. 2026 © Emerald Publishing Limited
journal: Higher Education, Skills and Work-based Learning
authors: Njøten, Håkon and Feyer, Frida K.
notes: Conceptual 4S framework paper. Preserve extension/modification and comparison of SEB/BESSI. No participant/sample extraction.
